description: Sifting Skies is an interactive viewer for finding clues in NASA’s SPHEREx infrared images. Blink between aligned images of the same patch of sky to see what moved or changed brightness, follow known objects like Vesta, or run an automated search that flags potential movers for you to review.
summary:
Sifting Skies is an interactive viewer for exploring NASA’s SPHEREx infrared observations. Enter right ascension and declination, choose a field of view, and play images of the same patch of sky in sequence to see what changes. You can scan for possible moving objects, review the frames behind each candidate, and overlay Gaia reference stars to judge whether a source shifts relative to its neighbours.

Measure brightness at a fixed position across dates to see whether a source brightens or fades, or draw a circle on an image to generate a spectrum across 102 infrared channels and see where the region emits more strongly. Some examples are Barnard’s Star, the Epsilon Indi B brown-dwarf pair, the fast-moving brown dwarf WISE 0855, or the variable stars RW Aurigae and R Draconis. You can also search your own sky field, include newer IRSA observations, and save a region to revisit.
details:
Sifting Skies

NASA Space Apps 2026 · Planet X and SPHEREx

Sifting Skies is a public-facing web tool for exploring how the infrared sky changes over time. Enter a right ascension, declination, and field of view, and the viewer retrieves NASA SPHEREx images of that patch of sky. Play them in sequence or blink between aligned exposures to see whether a source shifts relative to nearby stars.

What you can do

Workflow

What it does and why it matters

Validate a known object

Start with curated examples such as Vesta, Arosa, M101, or Barnard’s Star. Aligned images and Gaia reference stars help you distinguish apparent motion from shifts between images.

Explore for movement

Search your own sky field, optionally filter by detector, and use the timeline or autoplay to browse exposures as they arrive.

Static analysis

Circle a stationary region to see where it emits more strongly or weakly across 102 infrared channels. Inspect individual channel measurements or save the region as a Known Object in your browser.

Object detection & measurements

Run Auto observation to rank possible moving tracks. Review the exposures behind each candidate and measure its brightness along its estimated path.

Brightness measurement

Compare brightness at a fixed sky position across dates and similar wavelengths to look for brightening or fading. RW Aurigae and R Draconis offer guided examples.

How we built it

We built the viewer in React and TypeScript, with a Python and FastAPI backend. The backend queries NASA’s IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), retrieves FITS cutouts for the requested field, and uses astronomical coordinate metadata to align exposures and measure light at the selected positions. The frontend brings the images, timeline, spectra, and measurements into one browser interface.

Design choices and intended impact

We designed Sifting Skies to make archive data approachable for students, educators, and curious members of the public. Its central idea is to make the image itself the starting point for investigation. Notice a shift while blinking, inspect the frames that support a candidate track, or circle a stationary region and see how its light varies with wavelength.

We considered the trade-off between wider fields of view, which can help keep faster-moving sources in view, and longer download times. The app retrieves field cutouts on demand, shows frames as they arrive, and lets users include newer IRSA observations in Explore. We also keep the supporting frames and measurement details visible so users can judge the evidence for themselves. A candidate track is a starting point for investigation, and brightness comparisons are most meaningful across similar wavelengths.
